name: Mary I
summary: Mary I asserted her right to the throne by inheritance and coronation, and set out to reverse the religious changes of her father and brother, restoring papal authority and Catholic worship. She revived the heresy laws, under which about 280 Protestants were burned, and married Philip of Spain despite the unpopularity of the match and a rebellion against it. Her recorded words on politics are mostly about her title, her marriage and obedience, so many topics remain without a known position.

abolish-ip.rationale: The Stationers’ Company charter made enforcement of exclusive printing privileges part of the Crown’s regulation of the book trade.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Mary revived laws against heresy and her reign saw Cranmer executed after he repudiated his Catholic recantations. The law targeted departure from Catholic orthodoxy as heresy, so the fit to a general ban on leaving one’s religion is limited.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Mary made plays, ballads and rhymes subject to express royal authorization in a proclamation that treated unauthorized religious teaching and seditious performances as harms to public order.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Mary directed the bishop of London and his officers to carry out her reforms throughout his diocese. Her heresy statute restored diocesan authorities’ power to proceed against alleged heretics.

conscription.rationale: Mary issued orders for mustering men for the army at the siege of Calais, and a royal order to London directed a levy for the relief of Calais.

death-penalty.rationale: Mary’s government executed Lady Jane Grey and the leaders of Wyatt’s rising after convictions for treason.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Mary’s accession proclamation treated her title as hers by right on her brother’s death and called for allegiance on that basis.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Mary’s 1554 statute gave male and female sovereigns identical powers to exercise every function of the Crown.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Mary’s accession proclamation attributes the succession to divine providence and presents her claim as a lawful inheritance that obliges her subjects’ allegiance.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Mary’s marriage settlement expressly provided that children of the marriage would succeed to her realms under their succession laws and customs.

elective-rulers.rationale: Mary proclaimed her own accession as a legal right on Edward VI’s death. Her marriage settlement provided for the succession of her children under the laws of inheritance.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: In 1558 Mary placed possession of prohibited heretical and seditious books under martial law by proclamation.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The Spanish marriage settlement reaffirmed a perpetual confederacy and mutual aid under the earlier treaties with Charles V. Mary subsequently entered the war against France on Spain’s side.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Leix plantation Mary approved subjected Irish and English inhabitants to different legal rules for keeping arms. It restricted the Irish from holding firearms without a license and required English settler households to keep arms.

harm-principle.rationale: Mary subjected religious preaching, interpretation of scripture even in private settings, and printing to royal control, and her heresy settlement penalized doctrinal dissent.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Mary’s signed Framlingham proclamation ordered her subjects to join the royal army she had assembled under her lieutenant, the Earl of Sussex.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: Mary dissolved her third Parliament in January 1555 after it passed the statutes restoring papal jurisdiction and reviving the heresy laws.

indigenous-internal-justice.rationale: The Marian settlement required the O’Mores in the Irish part of Leix to use only common law, replacing their right to administer justice according to their own customs.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Mary approved a plantation that vested Leix and Offaly in the Crown and subjected the Irish holdings reserved in Leix to tenures and conditions laid down by the Crown administration.

majority-settlement.rationale: Mary’s Irish administration seized Leix and Offaly and put the districts under Crown plantation, granting confiscated land to settlers and reserving fortified towns for the new administration.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Mary committed England to war against France in 1557 alongside Philip, sending English forces to take part in his campaign in France.

minority-language-support.rationale: Under the Leix plantation Mary approved, Irish tenants had to teach their children English and settlers risked forfeiture for abandoning English.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: The Crown turned Leix and Offaly into shires. In the parts of Leix set aside for the O’Mores, their chiefs held land under Crown tenure and were required to use English common law.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: Mary contracted with mint officers to issue coins under specified gold and silver fineness and weight standards.

more-religion-public.rationale: Mary restored Catholic worship by repealing Edward VI’s religious settlement and ordered the Bishop of London to enforce her religious reforms throughout his diocese.

national-church-status.rationale: The repeal acts restored the Catholic church’s public worship and jurisdiction, and a separate statute supplied legal sanctions against doctrines outside its teaching.

native-born-offices.rationale: The marriage settlement reserved English and dependent territories’ offices and benefices to persons born in the relevant realms and barred Philip from appointing foreigners to them.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Mary’s enactments made enforcing religious doctrine and restoring ecclesiastical jurisdiction functions of the Crown and government.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Mary chartered the Stationers’ Company with exclusive printing privileges, subject to separate royal licenses, and with Philip approved the Muscovy Company’s trading charter.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Mary’s articles ordered bishops to examine schoolmasters, remove those suspected of religious heterodoxy, and have Catholic replacements prepare pupils to assist at Mass.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Mary secured parliamentary statutes for the marriage settlement and religious restoration. Her own proclamations also imposed rules on printing and religious debate and directed detention for breach.

party-controls-media.rationale: Mary required written royal authorization to print books, ballads and rhymes. Her 1557 charter reserved most printing to members of the Stationers’ Company or holders of a royal license.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The Muscovy Company obtained defined commercial privileges and a prescribed corporate structure by royal charter. The Stationers’ Company’s royal charter confined printing to company members and independent holders of royal licenses.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Mary’s settlement restored Roman jurisdiction and revived statutes to enforce Catholic orthodoxy against rival Christian doctrines.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Mary restored laws allowing church authorities to proceed against adherents of competing religious doctrines, and Protestant religious practice was prosecuted under the settlement.

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: The Crown took land in Leix and Offaly for plantation. In Leix the settlers received the eastern district, with a portion of the western district reserved under new Crown tenures for members of the O’More clans.

restore-past-order.rationale: Her repeal acts reversed Edward VI’s church settlement and Henry VIII’s break with Rome, bringing back the earlier system of worship and ecclesiastical jurisdiction.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Mary’s revived heresy statutes gave church authorities power to prosecute those who adopted teachings outside Catholic orthodoxy.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Mary approved the plantation of Leix, under which English settlers received the eastern district and most areas were assigned according to terms set by her administration.

return-lost-territory.rationale: After France captured Calais in 1558, Mary pressed Philip and her council to recover it and sought its restoration in any peace.

separate-church-state.rationale: Mary used statutes to restore the authority of Rome and revive civil enforcement of Catholic orthodoxy through the heresy laws.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Mary accepted a statutory marriage settlement preserving the laws and customs of the realm and limiting what Philip could do as joint sovereign.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The plantation Mary approved in Leix required English settler households to keep arms, and imposed separate restrictions on the arms held by the Irish.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Mary used royal injunctions and acts of Parliament to restore Catholic worship and enforce its standards of religious conduct.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Mary assented to the repeal of royal supremacy and restored the jurisdiction of the See of Rome and the pre-schism jurisdiction of church courts, within the limits set out in the repeal act.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Mary’s proclamation against sedition put unauthorized plays and publications under royal license and directed officers to detain deliberate offenders. She also imprisoned Elizabeth on suspicion of involvement in Wyatt’s rebellion.

notes: Mary’s August 1553 proclamation promised temporary forbearance in matters of conscience while imposing immediate controls on preaching, publication and private reprisals. Her subsequent statutes restored Roman jurisdiction and made religious conformity enforceable. Both the August proclamation and the March 1554 royal instructions are available in full transcriptions. This pass reviewed the full statement bank and checked religious policy, the royal succession, parliamentary power, press regulation, war, diplomacy, coinage, trade and the Irish plantations. Follow-up for the widest uncertainty lines used the marriage statute and trading charter, the Irish plantation terms, and work on Tudor customs, textiles, grain provisioning and poor relief. The evidence on customs describes a revenue measure and does not establish a protective tariff policy, and the evidence on labour and relief does not settle the statements on class relations. Earlier source IDs are retained for the signed answer history.
